conj: Conjecture: for each positive integer k, the sequence defined by a(n) (mod k) is eventually periodic with period dividing phi(k). For example, modulo 13 the sequence becomes [1, 8, 1, 9, 12, 10, 0, 8, 1, 9, 12, 10, 0, ...]; after the initial term 1 this appears to be a periodic sequence of period 6, a divisor of phi(13) = 12. - _Peter Bala_, Dec 11 2021
Conjecture: For any prime p > 3 with p == 3 (mod 8), we have 2*h(-p)*sqrt(p) = Sum_{k=1..(p-1)/2} csc(2*Pi*k^2/p). - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Aug 06 2019
Conjecture: a(p*n) = a(n) (mod p^2) for prime p = 1 (mod 4) and all positive integers n. Cf. A004982 and A298799. - _Peter Bala_, Dec 22 2019
Conjecture: a(p*n) = a(n) (mod p^2) for prime p == 1 (mod 4) and all positive integers n. Cf. A004981. - _Peter Bala_, Dec 22 2019
Conjecture: a(n) = A008837(n) = p*(p-1)/2 = Sum_{k=0..p-1} mod(k^3, p) where p = prime(n). - _Michael Somos_, Feb 17 2020
Conjecture: a(n) != -1 (mod n) for a composite n. - _Thomas Ordowski_, Jun 11 2025
Conjecture: Odd primes p such that 1^(p-1) + 2^(p-1) + ... + (p-1)^(p-1) == p-1 (mod p^2). - _Thomas Ordowski_ and _Giovanni Resta_, Jul 25 2018
Conjecture: the Gauss congruences a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^k) hold for all primes p and positive integers n and k. Cf. A185895. - _Peter Bala_, Mar 17 2022
Conjecture: a composite n is a Giuga number if and only if Sum_{k=1..n-1} k^lambda(n) == -1 (mod n), where lambda(n) = A002322(n). - _Thomas Ordowski_ and _Giovanni Resta_, Jul 25 2018
Conjecture: For any m = 1, 2, 3, ... and r = 0, ..., m - 1, there are infinitely many positive integers n with a(n) == r (mod m). - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Feb 27 2013
Conjectures: the supercongruences a(p) == -1 - p (mod p^2) and a(2*p) == p - 1 (mod p^2) hold for all primes p >= 3. - _Peter Bala_, Apr 18 2023

Conjecture: Each residue class contains infinitely many terms of this sequence. Similarly, for any integers m > 0 and r, we have prime(n) + n == r (mod m) for infinitely many positive integers n. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Nov 25 2013
Conjectures: a(5*n+3) == 0 (mod 5), a(5*n+4) == 0 (mod 5) and a(5*n+2) - 2*a(5*n+1) == (0 mod 5) (all checked up to n = 49). - _Peter Bala_, Jun 19 2023

Conjecture: lim n -> infinity a(n)/n = C exists and 4 < C < 9/2. There seems to be a sequence of primes p such that p^2 never divides numbers of the form 2^x + 1: the first few are 2, 7, 23, 31. - _Benoit Cloitre_, Aug 20 2002
Conjecture: for n > 2, this is the least prime p such that 1^2, 2^2, 3^2, ..., n^2 are distinct mod p. Checked to 10^4. - _Charles R Greathouse IV_, Dec 03 2022
Conjecture: except a(1)=3, a(n) is congruent 7 (mod 8). - _Ralf Stephan_, May 23 2026
Conjectures: a(n) == 1 (mod 80); for fixed k, the sequence a(n) (mod k) eventually becomes periodic. - _Peter Bala_, Dec 19 2019

Conjectures: a(2*n) = 3 (mod 60) and a(2*n+1) = 1 (mod 60); for fixed k, the sequence a(n) (mod k) eventually becomes periodic with exact period a divisor of phi(k), where phi(k) is Euler's totient function A000010. - _Peter Bala_, Feb 04 2018
Conjecture: All the terms are divisible by 10 (tested on the first 10^6 terms). - _Amiram Eldar_, Oct 19 2019

Conjecture: for fixed k = 1,2,..., the sequence a(n) (mod k) is eventually periodic with the exact period dividing phi(k), where phi(k) is the Euler totient function A000010. For example, modulo 10 the sequence becomes (1, 1, 5, 9, 1, 1, 5, 9, ...), with an apparent period 1, 1, 5, 9 of length 4 = phi(10) beginning at a(0). - _Peter Bala_, Jan 15 2018
Conjecture: these are composites k such that 2^M(k-1) == -1 (mod M(k)^2 + M(k) + 1), where M(k) = 2^k - 1. - _Amiram Eldar_ and _Thomas Ordowski_, Dec 19 2019
Conjecture: a(n) = 0 if and only if n > 2 and n == 2 mod 5 (which makes 2*n+1 == 0 mod 5). - _Robert Israel_, May 26 2015

Conjecture (seems provable): More generally let a and b(1) be integers. If b(n+1) = b(n) + b(n) (mod(n+a)) there is an integer x(a,b(1)) such that b(n+1) = b(n) + x(a,b(1)) for n sufficiently large. We have x(0,1) = x(1,1) = x(2,1) = 97, x(3,1) = 1, x(4,1) = 3, x(5,1) = 3, x(6,1) = 6, ..., x(97,1) = 43, x(0,11) = 2, etc. - _Benoit Cloitre_, Aug 20 2002

Conjecture: a(n) is the largest prime p <= 2n+1 such that p * A000367(n) == - A002445(n) (mod p^2) for n > 0. Note that 2^(2n) == 1 (mod a(n)), since a(n) is the largest prime p such that b^(2n)== 1 (mod p) for every b coprime to p; i.e., a(n) is the largest prime p such that p-1 | 2n. - _Thomas Ordowski_, May 17 2020
Conjecture: Let f(a,b)=1, if (a+b) mod |a-b| != (a mod |a-b|)+(b mod |a-b|), and 0 otherwise. a(n) = Sum_{k=1..n-1} f(n,k). - _Benedict W. J. Irwin_, Sep 22 2016
Conjecture: Let f(a,b)=1, if (a+b) mod |a-b| != (a mod |a-b|)+(b mod |a-b|), and 0 otherwise. a(n) = Sum_{k=1..n-1} f(n+k,n-k). - _Benedict W. J. Irwin_, Sep 23 2016
Conjecture: Let f(a,b)=1, if (a+b) mod |a-b| != (a mod |a-b|)+(b mod |a-b|), and 0 otherwise. a(n) = Sum_{k=1..n-1} 1-f(n,k). - _Benedict W. J. Irwin_, Sep 22 2016
Conjecture: all numbers at even positions are congruent 2 (mod 3). - _Ralf Stephan_, May 23 2026

Empirically, the points lie roughly on two lines: if n == 2 mod 3 then a(n) ~= 2n/3, otherwise a(n) ~= 4n/3. See A249680-A249683 for the three trisections, and see also the Sigrist scatterplot. - _N. J. A. Sloane_, Nov 03 2014, Nov 04 2014
Conjecture: For any odd prime p, we have a(p) == -1/2 (mod p). - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Aug 30 2021
a(n) = 1 if n == 1 (mod 3).
a(n) = 2 if n == 2 (mod 3).
Conjecture: a(42 + 6*k) = 0.  This would follow from the conjecture that for n >= 67, A103683(n) is divisible by 3 iff n == 3 mod 4 and by 2 iff n == 2 mod 4. - _Robert Israel_, May 12 2015
Conjecture: for n > 3, numerator(-2/n + Sum_{k=1..n} 2^k/k) == 0 (mod n^2) if and only if n is prime. See my formula below. Cf. A332786. - _Thomas Ordowski_, Mar 02 2020
Conjecture: a(5*n+4) == 0 (mod 5) (checked up to n = 200). - _Peter Bala_, Feb 26 2021
Conjecture: the supercongruence a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^(2*k)) holds for all primes p >= 5 and positive integers n and k. - _Peter Bala_, Aug 29 2025
Conjecture: the supercongruence a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^(2*k)) holds for all primes p >= 5 and positive integers n and k. - _Peter Bala_, Aug 29 2025
Conjecture: the supercongruence a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^(2*k)) holds for all primes p >= 5 and positive integers n and k. - _Peter Bala_, Aug 29 2025
Conjecture: a(n) is the smallest prime p such that Sum_{k=1..n} k^(p-1) == n (mod p). Thus a(n) >= A317358(n). - _Thomas Ordowski_, Jul 29 2018
Conjecture: a(n) is divisible by 4 iff n is divisible by 3, otherwise a(n) == 2 (mod 4) for n > 1 with a(1) = 1. - _Paul D. Hanna_, Apr 03 2026
Conjecture: if 3 does not divide n then n^2 divides a(n). - _Peter Bala_, Jul 24 2025

Conjecture: the supercongruences a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^(3*k)) hold for primes p >= 5 and positive integers n and k. Extending the sequence to negative n via a(-n) = Sum_{k = 0..n} C(-n,k)^4 * Sum_{j = 0..k} C(k,j)^4 produces the sequence [1, 3, 1491, 1663491, 2742551763, 5400215949753, 12106456954153971, 29631476653021123107, ...], which appears to satisfy the same supercongruences. Cf. A141057. - _Peter Bala_, Aug 05 2026
Conjecture: a(n) is the smallest integer k > 1 such that 2^(k-1) == 1 (mod a(0)*...*a(n-1)*k), with a(0) = 1. - _Thomas Ordowski_, Mar 13 2019
Conjecture: the supercongruence a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^(3*k)) holds for all primes p >= 5 and positive integers n and k. - _Peter Bala_, Aug 04 2026
Conjecture: a(n) is never congruent to 3 modulo 4; see A218622. - _Paul D. Hanna_, Nov 03 2012
Conjectures: a(5*n+4) == 0 (mod 5) and a(7*n+5) == 0 (mod 7) (both checked up to n = 200). - _Peter Bala_, Feb 26 2021
Conjectures: a(5*n+4) == 0 (mod 5) and a(7*n+5) == 0 (mod 7) (both checked up to n = 200). - _Peter Bala_, Feb 26 2021
Conjecture: a(n) == 1 (mod 3) for n >= 1. - _Paul D. Hanna_, Dec 01 2024
Conjecture: a(5*n+4) == 0 (mod 5) (checked up to n = 200). - _Peter Bala_, Feb 26 2021
Conjectures: a(25*n+24) == 0 (mod 25) (checked up to n = 50) and a(7*n+5) == 0 (mod 7) (checked up to n = 200). - _Peter Bala_, Feb 26 2021
Conjecture: for r >= 2, and all primes p >= 5, a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r+3)). - _Peter Bala_, Oct 13 2022
Conjecture 1.1 of Osburn and Sahu is if p is a prime and JacobiSymbol(p, 23) = 1 and n>0 then a(n * p) == a(n) (mod p). - _Michael Somos_, Sep 21 2013
Conjecture: if p is a prime in A105874 then a(p-1) == 0 (mod p^2) (checked up to p = 24239 = A105874(1000)). - _Peter Bala_, Sep 19 2025
Conjecture: the supercongruences a(n*p^r) == a(n*p^(r-1)) (mod p^(3*r)) hold for all primes p >= 5 and all positive integers n and r. - _Peter Bala_, Jun 22 2023
Conjecture: the supercongruences a(p-1) == 1 (mod p^4) holds for all primes p >= 5 and a(p^2-1) == 1 (mod p^5) holds for all primes p >= 3. - _Peter Bala_, Mar 22 2023
Conjecture: primes p such that p^4 divides a(p) are the Wolstenholme primes A088164. - _Amiram Eldar_ and _Thomas Ordowski_, Jan 15 2020
Conjecture 1 is false.  It appears that for n => 13, a(n) = 3 for n == 1 (mod 4) and a(n) = 4 otherwise. - _Robert Israel_, May 29 2017
Conjecture: If n is divisible by 5 then a(n) > 0. - _Robert Israel_, Jan 23 2024
Conjecture: there are no numbers k in this sequence such that, for each prime factor q of 2^k - 1, q == 1 (mod k). - _Thomas Ordowski_, Sep 20 2017
Conjecture: a(n+k) == a(n) (mod k) for all n and k. If true, then for each k, the sequence a(n) taken modulo k is a periodic sequence and the period divides k. - _Peter Bala_, Mar 12 2023

Conjecture: a(p*n) == a(n) (mod p^2) for prime p == 1 (mod 9) and all positive integers n except those n of the form n = m*p + k for 0 <= m <= (p-1)/9 and 1 <= k <= (p-1)/9. Cf. A034171, A004981 and A004982. - _Peter Bala_, Dec 23 2019

Conjecture: Let r(k) = the smallest positive residue of A003095(6*k+1) mod 10^(6*k+1). Then the first 2*k + 2 digits of r(k), reading from right to left, give the first 2*k + 2 digits of this 10-adic number. For example with k = 5, r(k) = 2121286728960294(201588948901) gives the first 12 digits correctly. - _Peter Bala_, Nov 14 2022

Conjecture: all odd terms {3, 5, 9, 13, 15, 21, 35, 39, 45, 63, 65, 91, 105, 117, 195, 273, 315, 455, 585, 819, 1365, 4095} are odd numbers k such that gpf(2^m-1) = gpf(m+1), where m = A002326((k-1)/2) is the multiplicative order of 2 mod 2k+1. - _Amiram Eldar_, Apr 15 2020
Conjecture: a(p-1) == 0 (mod p^2) for all primes p >= 5 (checked up to p = 499). - _Peter Bala_, Oct 23 2022
Conjecture: a(n) == 1 mod 406 for n > 5. - _Chai Wah Wu_, Oct 07 2020
Conjecture: a(p^r) == 1 (mod p^(2*r)) for positive integer r and all primes p >= 5. - _Peter Bala_, Mar 11 2024
Conjecture: for k a positive integer, the sequence {a(k^n): n >= 1} is a strong divisibility sequence; that is, for n, m >= 1,  gcd(a(k^n), a(k^m)) = a(k^gcd(n,m)). - _Peter Bala_, Dec 03 2022
Conjecture: for r >= 2, and all primes p >= 5, a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) ( mod p^(3*r+3) ). - _Peter Bala_, Oct 13 2022
Then b(n) = V(i) + f(j), where f(0) ... f(5) are 0,1,2,3,3,3, and for j >= 6, f(j) = 2 + 2*floor((j-2)/4) + epsilon(j), where epsilon(j) is 1 if j==1 mod 4 and is otherwise 0.
Conjecture: for r >= 2, a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) ( mod p^(3*r+3) ) for all primes p >= 5. - _Peter Bala_, Oct 13 2022
Conjecture: a(p^r) == a(p^(r-1)) ( mod p^(3*r+3) ) for r >= 2 and all primes p >= 5. - _Peter Bala_, Oct 26 2022
Conjecture: all terms are congruent 19 (mod 24). - _Ralf Stephan_, May 23 2026
Conjecture: the superconguence a(2*p-1) == 1 (mod p^3) holds for all primes p >= 5 (checked up to p = 101). - _Peter Bala_, Mar 20 2023
Conjecture: a(n) == A361552(n+1) (mod 4) for n >= 0. - _Paul D. Hanna_, Mar 19 2023

Conjecture 1: For all i, j, T(i,j) differs from its eight neighbors by at most 3. The array of differences {T(i+1,j) - T(i,j)} might be worth studying, as well as the array {T(i,j) mod 2}. - _N. J. A. Sloane_, Feb 25 2023
